lesson.title: Nothing Lost, Nothing Gained: The Law of Conservation of Mass
lesson.summary: In any ordinary chemical reaction, including a redox reaction, the total mass of the reactants equals the total mass of the products, because atoms are only rearranged, never created or destroyed.
lesson.body:
Conservation of mass is one of the oldest and most tested laws in chemistry: matter is neither created nor destroyed in a chemical reaction, it is only rearranged. This is a specific case of the broader conservation laws you have already encountered, applied here to the total mass of a chemical system. It is also the entire reason balancing equations, matching atom counts on both sides using coefficients, is not just a formatting convention. A properly balanced equation respects conservation of mass by construction, since the same atoms that start on the reactant side are still present, just recombined, on the product side.

Redox reactions involve electrons changing hands, which might make you wonder whether mass conservation still holds exactly. It does. An electron's mass is roughly 1800 times smaller than a proton's, small enough that moving a handful of electrons between atoms changes the total mass of a chemical sample by an amount far too tiny to detect on ordinary laboratory balances. What changes in a redox reaction is charge distribution among atoms, not the total mass of the system, so conservation of mass applies to redox equations exactly the same way it applies to any other reaction type.

Check this numerically using the magnesium and oxygen redox reaction from earlier in this unit: 2Mg(s) + O2(g) is right arrow 2MgO(s). Using molar masses of Mg = 24.3 g/mol, O2 = 32.0 g/mol, and MgO = 40.3 g/mol, compute the total mass on each side. Reactants: 2 mol of Mg contributes 2 x 24.3 = 48.6 g, plus 1 mol of O2 at 32.0 g, for a total of 48.6 + 32.0 = 80.6 g. Products: 2 mol of MgO contributes 2 x 40.3 = 80.6 g. The reactant mass, 80.6 g, equals the product mass, 80.6 g, exactly. That match is not a coincidence, it is guaranteed by the fact that the same atoms, 2 magnesium and 2 oxygen, appear on both sides of a correctly balanced equation.

This law is also what makes stoichiometry calculations work at all: because mass, and more precisely the number of atoms of each element, is conserved, you can use the mass of one substance in a reaction to calculate the mass of another. It is also directly testable in the lab. If you carry out a reaction in a sealed container and weigh it carefully before and after, the total mass measured will match, within the limits of your balance, confirming the law rather than merely assuming it.
